Advisory Opinion No. 24-03: Application of Public Officers Law § 74 to
employees of a State agency who have
formed a not-for-profit corporate entity
whose purpose is to solicit and accept
private sector contributions of gifts to the
agency in support of the agency’s mission.
INTRODUCTION
The following advisory opinion is issued by the New York State Commission on Ethics
and Lobbying in Government (the “Commission”), pursuant to Executive Law § 94(7)(c), in
response to an inquiry from the Ethics Officer at the New York State Department of Environmental
Conservation (the “Department”). Two employees of the Department had founded a not-for-profit
corporate entity called The Forest Ranger Foundation, Inc. (the “Foundation”), and had made
requests to the Department for approval to serve as officers of the Foundation. The purpose of the
Foundation includes collecting donations of “funding to provide innovative and cutting-edge
technology, equipment, supports, and services for Forest Rangers . . . that may otherwise be
unavailable or inaccessible due to limited funding and/or process restrictions . . . ”1 Forest Rangers
are employees of the Department.
The two employees are not policymakers, so their requests for approval of the outside
activity fell under the discretion of the Department as the employing agency.2 Given the novelty
of the situation, the Department’s Ethics Officer requested an informal opinion from Commission
staff as to whether the requests for approval of the outside activities could be granted, as well as
whether, and how, the Foundation could make donations to the Department. However, as this is a
matter of first impression, and there is no existing Commission precedent directly on point, the
Commission is releasing this formal Advisory Opinion holding that, absent explicit authorization

2 See Title 19 NYCRR Part 932.5. The approval process outlined in the outside activity regulations apply only to
policymakers, many of whose outside activities are subject to further review by the Commission. The outside
activities of non-policymakers are subject to review pursuant to the policies and procedures of the employing

2
from the agency to do so, Public Officers Law § 74(3)(d) and (h) prohibit State employees from
engaging in organized efforts to solicit and accept gifts to their employing agency. While the
motives of the employees in question appear to be commendable, permitting such activities will
reasonably create an impression among the public that the employees, or the agency, are engaged
in an artful tactic to benefit themselves. There is no provision in the law that permits State
employees, on their own initiative, to directly solicit or accept gifts on behalf of their employing
agency. The establishment and operation of the Foundation also interferes with the Department’s
normal governance and decision-making processes as the Foundation will constitute a separate
decision-making body aimed at affecting operations of the Department.
BACKGROUND
The Department’s Ethics Officer contacted Commission staff with an inquiry about two
applications the agency had received for outside activity approval. Two of the Department’s
employees had founded a not-for-profit entity – the Foundation – without prior notice to the
Department, and now sought approval from the Department to sit on the Foundation’s Board of
Directors.
Pursuant to its Certificate of Incorporation, the Corporation’s mission statement is as
follows:
The Corporation is formed for the purpose of lessening the burdens of government
by fostering, encouraging, and promoting private sector support for the New York
State Forest Rangers and providing such support to and for the New York State
Forest Rangers and its governmental purposes as part of the Division of Forest
Protection of the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.3
The following specific purposes are listed in the Certificate of Incorporation:
(1) Secure funding to provide innovative and cutting-edge technology, equipment,
supports, and services for Forest Rangers in furtherance of such purposes that
may otherwise be unavailable or inaccessible due to limited government
funding and/or process restrictions;
(2) Ensure Forest Rangers have access to the highest quality education and training
possible in order to assure their safety and ability to provide public safety and
state land protection through expertise in wildland search, rescue, fire, law
enforcement, and incident management throughout the State of New York;
(3) Conduct any and all lawful activities which may be necessary or useful in
furtherance of these stated purposes.4
In furtherance of such purposes, the Corporation may expend, contribute, disburse,
and otherwise dispose of its funds, income and other property by making grants and
contributions to, and cooperating with and otherwise voluntarily financially
assisting directly or indirectly such persons, any government entity including, but
not limited to, the Division of Forest Protection of the New York State Department
3 Fourth Clause, Certificate of Incorporation.
4 See, Id.(emphasis supplied).

3
of Environmental Conservation . . .5
The Foundation is governed by a Board of Directors of up to nine directors, all of whom
must be “currently employed by the Division of Forest Protection of the New York State
Department of Environmental Conservation as an entry-level Forest Ranger.”6 Directors earn no
salary or compensation other than entitlement to reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses,7 and
the Foundation is not to be used “for the pecuniary profit or financial gain of its directors or
officers.”8 The Foundation, and the participation of individual Forest Rangers with the Foundation,
have not been formally endorsed or sanctioned by the Department.
APPLICABLE LAW
Public Officers Law § 74 sets forth the State Code of Ethics, which is intended to prevent
State officers and employees from engaging in conduct that present actual or apparent conflicts of
interest. Section 74(2) states the general rule: “No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should
have any interest, financial or otherwise, direct or indirect, or engage in any business or transaction
or professional activity or incur any obligation of any nature, which is in substantial conflict with
the proper discharge of his duties in the public interest.”
The Code of Conduct, in Subdivision 3 of Public Officers Law § 74, sets forth minimum
standards of conduct. Conduct that falls short of any of these standards presents a conflict of
interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest. The standards of conduct relevant to the present
inquiry include the following:
d. No officer or employee of a state agency . . . should use or attempt to use his official
position to secure unwarranted privileges or exemptions for himself or others.
h. An officer or employee of a state agency . . . should endeavor to pursue a course of
conduct which will not raise suspicion among the public that he or she is likely to be engaged in
acts that are in violation of his or her trust.
The gift restrictions are set forth in Public Officers Law § 73(5):
5. No . . . state officer or employee . . . shall, directly or indirectly:
(a) solicit, accept or receive any gift having more than a nominal value, whether in
the form of money, service, loan, travel, lodging, meals, refreshments,
entertainment, discount, forbearance or promise, or in any other form, under
circumstances in which it could reasonably be inferred that the gift was intended to
influence him or her, or could reasonably be expected to influence him or her, in
the performance of his or her official duties or was intended as a reward for any
official action on his or her part. No person shall, directly or indirectly, offer or
make any such gift to a statewide elected official, or any state officer or employee,

(b) solicit, accept or receive any gift, as defined in section one-c of the legislative
law, from any person who is prohibited from delivering such gift pursuant to section

infer that the gift was intended to influence him or her; or
(c) permit the solicitation, acceptance, or receipt of any gift, as defined in section

gift pursuant to section one-m of the legislative law to a third party including a
charitable organization, on such official's designation or recommendation or on his
or her behalf, under circumstances where it is reasonable to infer that the gift was
intended to influence him or her.
DISCUSSION
The key question presented is whether it is permissible for State employees, on their own
initiative, to create and sit on the board of a not-for-profit corporation whose purpose is to solicit
and accept gifts for their employing agency. The Commission has noted that it “conceives of few,
if any, circumstances in which the solicitation by a State officer or employee in his or her official
capacity of a personal gift of any value would be appropriate behavior or be authorized by the
provisions of Public Officers Law § 74.”9 A more difficult question arises when individual State
employees undertake efforts to solicit gifts for the ostensibly public purpose of supporting their
own employing agency. The Commission finds that such activity, while commendable on its face,
blurs the line between state and private interests, can give rise to confusion among the public, and
creates an appearance of a conflict of interest that violates Public Officers Law § 74.
The Department’s Commissioner is authorized by statute to “acquire real or personal
property, including acquisition by condemnation, appropriation, gift, grant, devise or bequest.”10
In Advisory Opinion No. 95-38, the State Ethics Commission held that the Department could
accept donations directly from individuals and businesses, but with important caveats:
The Commission concludes that DEC may accept donations from individuals,
businesses or organizations whose activities are subject to its jurisdiction. However,
it may not accept donations from individuals or entities under investigation by or
in litigation with the agency. Decisions as to the propriety of a donation must be
made by the Commissioner on a case-by-case basis, considering its source, timing
and amount. . .. DEC may not accept donations where the equipment or money
donated is conditioned upon its use in a particular geographic region.11
Moreover, the agency could not accept any donation that is conditioned upon its use in a
specific geographic region:
9 Advisory Opinion No. 94-16, p. 6 (italic added).
10 N.Y. Environmental Conservation Law § 3-0301(2)(l). There is no statutory provision permitting employees of
the Department independently to receive gifts for the Department.
11 Advisory Opinion No. 95-38, p. 6.

5
The Commission concludes that donations made to DEC must be available for
agency use as the Commissioner deems appropriate. To hold otherwise would
unduly restrict the Commissioner in applying agency resources as circumstances
require, and could result in those employed in certain DEC regions enjoying better
working conditions or having better equipment than those employed elsewhere. A
donor cannot, in essence, make a donation to DEC in exchange for better services
in its area. The Commissioner must be free to determine the allocation of the
agency's resources statewide based upon his or her best judgment.12
These restrictions leave no room for lower-level employees to act as intermediaries,
shielding donors and their gifts from scrutiny by the Commissioner. This additional layer interferes
with the Commissioner’s obligation to consider each donation on a case-by-case basis, and leaves
open the possibility that improper donations will be received, whether from ineligible donors or
others. Moreover, as the Foundation is specifically dedicated to supporting the Forest Rangers and
the Department’s Division of Forest Protection, its offers to the Department come with strings
attached that preclude their acceptance by the Department.
Additionally, the Department’s employees who serve on the board of the Foundation or as
its officers will both practically and legally have conflicting loyalties to the Department and the
public, on the one hand, and, on the other, to the Foundation, to which they will owe fiduciary
responsibilities. Although the employees are seeking, among other things, to improve the
Department’s capabilities and the working conditions of its employees (that is, themselves), that
is not to say that the interests of the Foundation are co-extensive with the interests of the
Department. To the contrary, it is inevitable that the interests of the Foundation, and consequently,
the interests of its officers and directors, will conflict, as the Foundation is directed, as defined by
its certificate of incorporation, to merely one aspect of the Department’s operations, while the
Department must balance and prioritize among all of its statewide responsibilities. The dual and
conflicting loyalties created are in contravention of Public Officers Law § 74.13
Finally, the activities of the Foundation are apt to give rise to confusion amongst the public
about its operations. Is the Foundation the same as or related to the Department? Does the
Foundation represent the Department? Why is the Department seeking donations? Why is the
Department using an independent entity to solicit donations? Are Department employees seeking
donations as state officers and employees of the Department or as agents of the Foundation? At
what point, if any, will the propriety of donations made to the Foundation, especially from donors
who have business before the Department, be assessed, and by whom? What authority does the
Foundation have with respect to the Department? What happens to donations that are declined by
the Department? The independent actions of the employees, which are not coordinated with the
Department, can create the impression that the employees are acting in pursuit of their own
interests, or the interests of the Foundation, rather than the best interests of the Department.

13 Advisory Opinion No. 99-04, p. 3.

6
CONCLUSION
Public Officers Law § 74(3)(d) and (h) prohibit the DEC employees from forming and
sitting on the board of a corporate entity whose mission is to receive or solicit public contributions
of money or equipment to benefit their employing agency. Any organized effort by agency
employees to solicit and/or receive donations to their employing agency must be explicitly
approved by their agency, and the solicitation efforts must clearly state (i) that the solicitation is
endorsed by the agency; (ii) the intended use of the contributions, (iii) an explanation of the
decision to seek these items or funds by donation, and (iv) that the agency will return any
contribution that, in its judgment, is improper. Further, the agency must consider each donation on
a case-by-case basis as set forth in Advisory Opinion No. 95-38.
